description:
Team from Poltava, Ukraine. We're building an interactive 3D navigator for the Moon's south pole: pick a landing site and a date, and see how much sunlight it gets and when Earth is in view for communication. More on the project page

Команда з Полтави, Україна. Ми створюємо інтерактивний 3D-навігатор для південного полюса Місяця: оберіть місце посадки й дату та побачте, скільки там Сонця і коли Земля в зоні видимості для звʼязку. Детальніше на сторінці проєкту

summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web tool that shows where and when to land near the lunar south pole. At the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a few hundred metres decide whether a lander gets power: within 500 m of Connecting Ridge, sunlight ranges from 38.5% to 87% of the time.

For any point and any dates, the app uses the real local horizon (NASA LOLA terrain, 1440 directions, rays up to 200 km) and NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE ephemerides to compute three numbers: Sun % (mean visible fraction of the solar disk), Earth % (share of time Earth is above the horizon for direct communication) and the longest night, which sets the battery size.

It shows 3D terrain with heat maps, compares two sites, finds the best spot within 5 km taking slope into account, and ranks landing windows by hours with both Sun and Earth visible. Every number is labelled with its period and panel/antenna height (default 2 m). Results are validated against NASA LOLA illumination maps (1.0 pp mean error over 150 points) and Gläser et al. 2018. Open source, Apache-2.0.
details:
Live app: https://space.mindal1ka.com · 30-second video: https://space.mindal1ka.com/video · Slides: https://space.mindal1ka.com/pitch · Code: https://github.com/Mindal1ka/lunar-site-navigator

The problem

On 6 March 2025 the IM-2 Athena lander touched down near the lunar south pole a few hundred metres from its target, in a crater, on its side. Its solar panels could not catch the low Sun and the mission ended after about 12 hours. At the pole the Sun moves along the horizon, so a ridge a few kilometres away can shadow a site for days. Static illumination maps average many years at ground level; a mission planner needs answers for a specific point, height and set of dates.

What it does

  • Three numbers for any point: Sun % (mean visible fraction of the solar disk), Earth % (share of time Earth is above the horizon plus an antenna margin, for direct-to-Earth links) and the longest night (longest interval with the Sun fully hidden).
  • When to land: the best 14-day landing window, ranked by the share of hours with Sun and Earth visible together, plus a planner for any window length.
  • Where to land: search for the best spot within 5 km, excluding steep slopes; compare two sites side by side.
  • Battery: load × longest night ÷ allowed depth of discharge (80 %).
  • 3D terrain with Sun, Earth, night and slope heat maps, the local horizon panorama, time-series charts and CSV export. Works in a browser, including phones. English and Ukrainian.
  • Every number on screen is labelled with how it is computed, the period, and the panel/antenna height (default 2 m, adjustable 0–20 m).

How it works

  • Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA south-polar DEM, 40 m/px for horizons and 80 m/px for 3D.
  • For each point the horizon is traced in 1440 directions (0.25°), along rays up to 200 km, with exact lunar curvature.
  • Sun and Earth positions come hourly from NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) in the same Moon frame as LOLA.
  • The visible part of the solar disk and Earth above the horizon are computed for every hour. The region-wide 100 m map (17.6 million points) is computed on a GPU in about 2 minutes; the app recomputes the selected site in the browser.

Validation

  • NASA LOLA average-visibility maps (same definition, same 0 m height): mean absolute error 1.0 percentage point for Sun and 1.2 pp for Earth over 150 random points.
  • Gläser et al. 2018 published illumination at the same heights: e.g. Connecting Ridge C2 78.0 vs 78.1 %, Shackleton rim 85.5 vs 85.5 %, C1 86.4 vs 88.0 %. The largest difference is shown openly in the app.
  • Sun/Earth geometry checked against JPL Horizons (max 0.1″). This checks frames and timing only, not independent accuracy.
  • Known limitation: at exactly 0 m on sharp ridges, results depend on terrain smaller than a pixel, so the app defaults to 2 m and says so.

Impact

Teams planning CLPS-class landers and student missions can choose a site and date with a known energy and communication budget, and see how sensitive the choice is to a landing error of a few hundred metres. For example, Connecting Ridge C1 gets 87 % Sun with a 9.1-day longest night, while the Athena landing site gets 47 % with a 17-day night.

Tools

Python (NumPy, Numba, SpiceyPy, CuPy) for the data pipeline; SvelteKit, TypeScript, three.js and uPlot for the web app. Open source under Apache-2.0.

Use of AI

An AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) helped write and review code, look up data formats, check calculations, write texts and translations, and build the slides and the video from real app screen captures. The idea, features and decisions are the team's. AI-assisted source files are marked in their headers and in the README. No AI-generated images are used; the video music was synthesized by our own code.
